name: Morrison
title: Artificial Turf in Morrison, CO | TIMELESS Grass & Greens
description: A backyard lawn, dog area or putting green in Morrison usually needs no Town application. What pulls a project into one, and how to check your address.
h1: Artificial turf in Morrison, CO, under a 2025 code that doesn't ban it.
lede: An existing-yard turf swap in Morrison usually stays outside the code's application rules; confirm yours with staff in writing. Book a free visit to measure and check the ground.
wins: A lawn, dog area or putting green reads as outdoor area, not a structure
Check the 2025 zoning map first — some Morrison addresses sit outside Town limits
A layout that stays clear of any subdivision or floodplain trigger

answer.question: Does Morrison, CO require a permit for artificial turf?
answer.answer: Not usually. Morrison's 2025 code bans artificial plants but not turf, and its application rules aim at new development, not a turf swap in an existing yard. Subdivision grading or new development on FEMA-mapped flood land can still pull a project in.

blocks.h2: Artificial turf isn't banned — and usually isn't a "structure" either.
blocks.takeaway: The 2025 code bans artificial plants but not turf, and a lawn fits its list of non-structures, like walks and paved areas, better than a building. New development needs at least 50 percent native plants.
paras: Morrison is a home rule town with its own land use rules. On 20 May 2025 the Board of Trustees voted to adopt Ordinance No. 553 and its new Land Use Code, according to that meeting's minutes. The landscaping section bans artificial trees, shrubs and plants, and adds in brackets that the ban doesn't include artificial turf.

The same code defines a "structure" as any piece of work artificially built up from parts joined together on the ground — but it excepts paved areas, walks, tennis courts and similar outdoor areas. A turf lawn, dog run or putting green fits that list better than it fits a building, which is why most of Title 10's application requirements, written around development and structures, don't have an obvious reason to reach an ordinary yard.

Where the code's landscaping rule can still reach a project: if it counts as new development or a subdivision under Article D for another reason (see below), at least 50 percent of the plants on the site must be native, and any non-native plant needs low water use, drought tolerance and freeze resistance. Our custom layout keeps the planting beds inside that rule when it applies.

blocks.kicker: When the code actually reaches your yard
blocks.h2: A backyard swap skips the inquiry form; an addition doesn't.
blocks.takeaway: An existing-yard turf swap doesn't fit the code's development triggers on its own; get staff to confirm that in writing. A new shed, subdivision grading or flood-hazard building starts with the inquiry form.
paras: Morrison's Planning & Zoning page says every planning and development application must start with a Planning & Development Inquiry Form, before you meet staff or apply. Read plainly, that's a rule about applications — and the code's own development standards apply to new development, subdivisions and Substantial Improvement, meaning work on a structure costing at least 30 percent of its market value. A lawn, dog area or putting green in an existing yard doesn't fit any of those on its own.

What does pull a project into an application: adding something that is a structure in its own right, such as a shed for equipment; grading done as part of a subdivision or site plan application, where the code's 3:1 slope limit and 20-foot terracing rule bind; or building on land FEMA maps as flood hazard, covered next. If your project is one of those, start with the inquiry form. If it's a straightforward yard, ask staff to confirm that reading and keep the answer in writing.

Development itself is any man-made change to improved or unimproved real estate, and staff decide within ten business days whether a submitted application is complete. None of that timeline starts unless something above actually applies to your project.

blocks.kicker: Bear Creek and the flood map
blocks.h2: On FEMA-mapped land, the floodplain permit comes before the dig.
blocks.takeaway: Along Bear Creek, reshaping ground on FEMA-mapped flood land can need a floodplain development permit before digging. Check the Town's map for your lot and ask through the inquiry form.
paras: George Morrison platted the town on Bear Creek in 1874, and today the Land Use Code maps a flood hazard area along that same creek (Wikipedia). The code requires a floodplain development permit before new development or Substantial Improvement in a special flood hazard area on FEMA's most recent maps, including land taken out of the floodplain by fill.

Development is any man-made change to real estate, so a project that reshapes the ground rather than resurfacing it in place could qualify. We couldn't confirm which Morrison lots sit inside the mapped area — the Town's map is the place to check, and the inquiry form is where you ask. Staff decide the permit, and an appeal goes to the Board of Trustees at a public hearing.

A designated floodway is stricter still: nothing new goes in unless an engineer's hydrologic and hydraulic analysis shows no rise in flood levels in the Town during the base flood. That's a narrow case, but if it applies to your lot, plan for it before anything else.

blocks.h2: Check the zoning map before the code — the ZIP reaches past Town limits.
blocks.takeaway: The 80465 ZIP reaches well past Town limits, so check the 2025 zoning map to see whether Town rules apply at all. Inside, the Town runs your water; ask Public Works about watering rules.
paras: The 80465 ZIP code reaches west up Turkey Creek Canyon and south of town, covering about 5,000 addresses, many of them in unincorporated Jefferson County (Wikipedia). Title 10 governs only lots inside the Town, so find yours on the 2025 Official Zoning Map before any of the rules above apply at all. A business in the Historic Downtown district should raise turf with staff before choosing a product.

The Town also runs your water and sewer. Its Public Works page says Bear Creek is the raw water source, treated at a membrane filtration plant, with two off-stream reservoirs for drought. Ask Public Works at 303-697-8749 about watering rules or conversion help; our water rebates guide shows which Denver-area providers pay toward turf.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Morrison, CO?
faq.a: We install artificial turf, pet turf, backyard putting greens and commercial turf in Morrison, CO. Book a free visit to measure and check the ground, and we'll draw a custom layout for you to approve before work starts. Call 303-349-2368.

faq.q: Does a backyard putting green count as a structure in Morrison?
faq.a: Probably not on its own. A structure is any piece of work built up from parts joined together on the ground, but paved areas, walks, tennis courts and similar outdoor areas are excepted, and a putting green fits that description. The code doesn't name putting greens directly, so if you want it in writing, ask on the inquiry form and keep the answer.

faq.q: Does artificial turf count as impervious surface in Morrison?
faq.a: The code doesn't name it. Impervious surface is anything artificially covered or hardened to impede water soaking in, and the examples include plastic and gravel. The stormwater rules apply to subdivision and site plan applications that add impervious area, so ask staff how they'd class a turf base that drains. Our impervious surface guide sets out the question.

faq.q: How tall can the fence around a Morrison dog run be?
faq.a: Six feet in a side or rear yard and four feet in front, plus two feet for a fence on top of a retaining wall. Don't run it across an open drainage channel or easement where it would restrict flow, unless the Town approves a revocable permit (Land Use Code). This rule stands on its own; it doesn't wait for a development application.

faq.q: Does state law limit turf at a Morrison business or HOA?
faq.a: Colorado law limits new nonfunctional artificial turf on commercial, institutional and common-interest community property, but only for new development and redevelopment — it doesn't reach an existing private home. Morrison's own code doesn't add a separate ban. Our Colorado turf law guide walks through what counts as functional turf.
